definition: Nascent means just coming into existence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word nascent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know nascent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The nascent hiking club had two members, a borrowed trail map, and a meeting spot that changed every week.
Growing goes further than nascent — a growing club already exists and is visibly gaining members, while a nascent one has only just come into being.
Thriving goes further than growing: not merely underway and expanding but flourishing, the fragile nascent stage long behind it.

Budding means already sprouted and visibly beginning to flourish — growth you can point to. Nascent sits one step earlier on the clock: the thing has only just come into existence and may have nothing to show yet. A budding club has momentum; a nascent one has barely crossed into being.

A fledgling venture is young and untried, wobbling through its first attempts — it already exists and is trying its wings. Nascent is earlier still: just coming into existence, before there are any attempts to wobble through. Call the idea's first week nascent and the shaky first season fledgling.

Nascent is the writer's word for the very first moments of something — a nascent industry, movement, rivalry.

When the Alvarez brothers registered their kelp farm, the industry around them was still nascent.
The state listed only three seaweed licenses, and the permitting rules were borrowed, clause by clause, from oyster law.
Buyers did not know what to pay, because almost nobody had ever sold a harvest.
The brothers spent their first winter writing definitions — what counts as a crop, what counts as a raft — for regulators who had never seen either.
Their rafts rode out two hurricanes that first year, and their father joked that you cannot join an industry that barely exists — you can only help it come into being.
